entry.title: Oh My Rockness Genre Enrichment
entry.content:
Oh My Rockness is a website that lists music shows in NYC. It also lets you filter by shows that are free to attend. I've never actually attended a show through the site, but I've wanted to.

My one qualm with it is that it does not easily show the genre of the bands or a description of the kind of music they play. There are so many event listings that it's hard to make a choice of which I might be interested in.

For a while, I've had an idea floating in my mind to create some way to easily tell what the genres of the bands are.

Today I decided to have an AI coding session to come up with a solution. And it worked out pretty well!

It scrapes from ohmyrockness as you flip through the dates, and pulls genre data from Spotify and Last.fm. Also includes a convenient link to the artist in Spotify. It took about an hour to spin this up.

It's locally only, and currently I don't plan to host it anywhere, but we'll see. For one thing, I'd worry that ohmyrockness would not be happy about a mirror of their site. Maybe a browser extension to augment the existing ohmyrockness site with genre data would be better than hosting a standaline webapp. But for now, this tool perhaps will be useful to me. (I do sense there is a flaw for my local setup in that it must be run on my laptop, and there may be times when I want to know about current music events from my phone while I'm on-the-go. Maybe I'll be motivated to host this somewhere small just for my own use.)

Anyone can set this up locally if desired -- you just need a Spotify and/or Last.FM API key. Note that Spotify API requires a premium account, but Last.FM is free and it should work with just that.

Note - this may be buggy and imperfect. Haven't tested it thoroughly.

Code is on Github: https://github.com/briancherin/ohmyrockness-genre-enrichment

entry.title: Good Luck, Have Fun, Don't Die (2025)
entry.content:
A wild ride of a movie. The focus is on anti-AI, anti-overconsumption, anti a world where the spirit of humanity becomes lost to technology. It's presented in an over-the-top way, so it's not as serious of a take on these issues in some ways, but this makes it enjoyable and entertaining while still posing deep questions. Similar feeling to Black Mirror. The cinematography is excellent. I was closely engaged for the whole movie and eager to see it through. During the first half, I thought it would end up being my favorite movie of this year... Maybe it still will be, but some flaws in the second half make me less confident in making such a claim.

Spoiler-full reactions below.

[!DANGER] Spoilers ahead.

[!DANGER] Spoilers ahead.

[!DANGER] Spoilers ahead.

[!DANGER] Spoilers ahead.

[!DANGER] Spoilers ahead.

  • The ending

    • The hesitation
      • He was able to plug the thing in, but then he hesitates for twenty seconds. It seemed like he could have plugged it in during those twenty seconds, but instead he stopped to watch what was happening (objects started flying in the air, but they weren't threatening yet). Clearly they needed him to not plug it in at that point so that Ingrid could be the one to go for it and then we get the reveal that she is the time traveler's mother. They could have paced that scene better so that he didn't have the unreasonable, unbelievable moment of hesitation. This alone knocks half a star off my rating for this movie.
      • That being said, twist #2 (they actually lost) revealed that the safeguards didn't actually change anything. So the hesitation didn't actually matter ultimately, and in fact perhaps did show to time traveler that this approach will never work. I just wish the hesitation was more plausible. Did he really just freeze up? The scene did not set it up in that way.
    • Twist and double twist. I was not too pleased with the first twist (she is his mother), but was decently redeemed by the second twist (the safeguards didn't actually help; their reality is being manipulated; they really lost).
      • Her being his mother... I had thought the future he came from was much further into the future, not max ~50 years ahead. Maybe it makes sense.
    • I'm pleased with the very ending -- the new idea to spread her technology allergy. Who knows if it's the thing that will actually save the world, but I like that the whole plot of the movie led up to scrapping the premise (the original heist idea) and using what was learned to get to a next step that we don't actually see.
    • But also, maybe it's not the ending we as an audience, dealing with similar issues in the real world, want. Or at least I don't. We don't want to be forced to not use any technology. We would rather have guardrails. But that's the idea of the ending. It poses that guardrails will never be enough; technology will always corrupt. The only way to avoid that is to avoid technology entirely. Do I believe this? Again, I don't really want to. But I think it's a reasonable hypothesis.

  • Open questions

    • We didn't get much info about the group of people that sent him to the past. He opens with the information that there is some grouping of people in the diner that will lead to a successful mission. How does he/anyone know that? (Does it have to do with Ingrid being his mother? Did he somehow know she had been there?) Did that only apply to the flash drive mission, or does that also apply to the new rat-spread-tech-allergy idea at the end?
    • Will the proposed solution at the end work? Who knows. But there is hope still.
    • What's the mechanism by which the AI/technology controls the people using it? The anti-phone ray guns show that when the tech turns off, the user seems to exit a trance state.

  • What was up with the mother's AI son helping the heist? Was that just the all-powerful AI luring them in so that it could get to Ingrid, make the son reveal, and try to convince her to stop the rebellion? (probably)

  • Not totally sure about why the AI is able to seemingly manipulate the real world like spawning the cat monster. Oh, I guess if there is technology to clone humans, they probably are advanced enough to make cat monsters that emit sparkles.

  • Dystopian concepts presented

    • Using AI voice to replace a lost child
    • Using AI-driven clones to replace a lost child. The clones spout product advertisements.
    • School shootings have become so commonplace that parents are numbed to it and are willing to replace their children with AI (truly absurd).
    • Teenagers behaving literally like zombies due to technology

  • Other notes

    • Feels like the writer is talking directly to audience when the time traveler explains the mission and the bad things about the future. Example at 53:00.
    • I like the junk build aesthetic. Like the anti-phone ray guns.
    • I like the "good luck have fun don't die" chorus sound and also the theme song.

  • Writer's message to the present world

    • Create AI guardrails before AI advances further

  • Parallels to my writing idea

    • One of my ideas for a story (not sure if short story or novel) is "Agents of Chaos", about time-looping agents who must complete missions to change how events turn out, and there are antagonistic forces trying to stop them. This movie had a similar core concept. Does this make me less interested in my own idea? Only time will tell. It perhaps slightly is off-putting to me, but I don't think I should let it and I don't necessarily think it will. My idea is different enough and generally I understand/believe that similar concepts can be manifested in different executions/styles/etc. I'm not claiming to be the sole inventor of a time looping idea at all. It seemed like a fun idea to me. Also my idea became quite sprawling, so I feel there's a lot of potential with it. (If I ever actually start writing it...)

  • Questions to think about

    • Effectiveness of the over-the-top ridiculousness of the plot, versus a more serious take?
    • Would I volunteer to participate at the diner?
    • What am i doing to fight against this future?
      • In my very small way:
        • Evading short-form content and instead cultivating rational, critical thinking-geared writing in this digital garden
        • Cultivating real life community and connections
    • Could a VR world where you are your perfect self really be a better reality? Could AI/VR/tech really get us there? (It's pretty abstract, the concept is so unimaginable I'm not sure how it could be answered.)

  • Read this review. I liked the ending note: "Everyone can align on the peril ahead as AI increasingly embeds itself in everyday life. How to meet this challenge with a new response remains tantalizingly just out of reach. Verbinski and Robinson’s cinematic equivalent of screaming “FIRE” in a crowded room might help the next person tackling this pressing topic find the exit.".

    • It feels like an important message to get out there and make art about. I'm curious how it will be represented in other media (whether future films, tv, or anything).

entry.title: Why do I stay vegan enough though I miss certain foods
entry.content:
No one has specifically asked me this question (not directly at least) but it kind of is a certain subtext to the vegan experience, so I will answer it.

The answer:
The intellectual and rational refusal to support animal exploitation/suffering/unnecessary_death far outweighs the sensation of satisfying the desire for this "missed" food item or any pleasure that might arise from consuming it.

It's not like I think about this much, though. I don't. It usually just surfaces when I'm around people eating non-vegan food and I would (pre-going-vegan) want to try it or share it, but obviously choose not to. For example, being with friends who are partaking in a cake makes me crave a cake. If the cake was vegan, I would obviously partake, and not think any different of it. So in this situation, it's not the non-vegan-ness of it (meaning, it's not that I find the vegan version inferior), but a matter of convenience and proximity. Of course, there are also foods that don't have quite good enough substitutes to really make me able to say the vegan option isn't inferior (e.g. not sure I've really ever found an adequate cheesecake substitute, yet)... So in a case like that, we go back to the "far outweighs" statement -- it's a very intentional choice to adhere to the philosophy of veganism and sacrifice what may be pleasure in satisfying a craving.

entry.title: Rick and Morty's Vegan Propaganda
entry.content:
Whoops, it's been two and a half years since I've watched a Rick and Morty episode! Back then, I had watched up through season 6. Then there was the wait for the next season, and I just never got back into it. But now apparently I'm in the mood for it again (and I'm over the fact that they changed the voice actor(s?) starting in S7 -- not that I disagree with their decision to do so, but it had me a little worried that the show would feel different).

FAQ:[1]

  1. Given this note's title, do I anticipate more examples of vegan propaganda in Rick & Morty? No, not necessarily, though I wouldn't be surprised. It's enough for me to start with the instance in S7 E4.
  2. "Vegan propaganda" ?? -- take this phrase lightly. It's obviously not actual propaganda. It's just how I'm describing media that has themes around exploitation, especially when it comes to food, and especially when it has a message that is sympathetic to those being exploited. And generally, yes, the exploited one would be an animal (though veganism at its core is against all exploitation, including of humans).
    • At least for me, being vegan means that these themes in media obviously stand out to me. But the message isn't always obvious to non-vegans.[2]

If you aren't familiar with Rick and Morty, and don't mind getting spoiled, feel free to read this. (But honestly, just watch the episode first!) It helps to have a sense of what kind of show Rick and Morty is (hint: weird, chaotic, cartoonishly gory, and often thought-provoking (and funny!)).

Warning: Spoilers for Rick and Morty Season 7 Episode 4

[!DANGER] Spoilers ahead.

[!DANGER] Spoilers ahead.

[!DANGER] Spoilers ahead.

[!DANGER] Spoilers ahead.

[!DANGER] Spoilers ahead.

But he was delicious. I hope that helps make it right.

The episode gets straight to the point.

It opens with the family eating Rick's delicious spaghetti with bolognese sauce. The family is raving about its deliciousness (and practically foaming at the mouth, with "sauce").

Pretty quickly, Morty finds out the secret to the deliciousness -- Rick has taken the "food" from the corpse of an alien (which closely resembles a human). Apparently, the people on the alien's planet turn into delicious spaghetti when they die, but only if they die of suicide (it's something specific to the biology of the people on that planet).

With that reveal, I started to sense that the vegan-adjacent themes. It's not about cannibalism (even though the alien looks like a human) because they are definitely not humans (humans don't turn into delicious spaghetti upon suicide; that's enough to differentiate the species[3]). The parallel to veganism so far is: You have a sudden realization about the food that you've been loving - it comes from a dark, morally-questionable place.

Morty feels bad about it. He insists that Rick tell him the name of the people they've been eating as spaghetti. They end up at the funeral of the spaghetti-man, and Morty speaks to the mourners:

Hi. I just want to be honest about something. After Lawrence died, we… …ate him. Wait, we’re not… werewolves or anything, we come from a planet, where to us, when you guys kill yourselves, you turn into what my planet considers food. Spaghetti. It brought us together. Lawrence. Brought us together. It just felt wrong not having anyone know that. But he was delicious. I hope that helps make it right.[4]

Morty genuinely feels bad about the whole situation. At the same time, he is unapologetic about enjoying the taste of the food.

I couldn't help but laugh at those last two sentence -- I was 100% sure that there were vegan undertones at this point. One of the most common reasons that people cite for not wanting (or not "being able") to go vegan, even when talked through a discussion of the moral wrongness of supporting an industry of unnecessary[5] animal suffering, is that meat (and other animal products) simply tastes too good for them to give it up. Any vegan will say that just because the animal "was delicious", it does not "make it right" to have killed them.

Ah, but here is the nuance of the Rick and Morty presentation of this topic -- as I write this, I realize that the nuance actually makes this less vegan propoganda than I might originally have framed it as. At the same time, the point I'm about to make does not negate the vegan theme, but rather approaches it from a slightly different angle than I was originally thinking.

These aliens don't have spaghetti inside them just by dying any death -- it has to be suicide. So they can't be farmed (raised and killed for their insides) in the same way that Earthly animals are. We've hit the topic of consent here. While the aliens are not necessarily given consent to be eaten (though this does come up later in the episode), they have chosen to die.

This changes everything.

Interlude: An Anecdote on Animal Suicide and Roadkill Meat

I didn't realize until getting to this point that I have a recent and relevant anecdote. But it's perfect.

A couple days ago, I was chatting with someone at a friend's birthday party. When it came up that I am vegan, he asked me if I would eat meat if the animal killed itself. I gave him a puzzled look and asked what animal would ever do that. He said something about pigs. My brief response pretty much was:

  1. it's ridiculous because animals have the biological instinct to survive (and, though it's apparently a bit controversial, there isn't evidence that any animals purposefully kill themselves), and
  2. even if the animal did intentionally kill itself, it has no way to communicate that intention to us humans, so we couldn't distinguish an intentional death from an unintentional one -- so this (unknowable) distinction would not be relevant to a decision on whether to eat a dead animal or not.

However -- it does bring up another relevant question. Would I (or vegans in general) eat an animal if it died accidentally? An actual example would be roadkill -- e.g. a deer hit by a car.

Some vegans will just say: no, it's an animal, and vegans don't eat animals, regardless of how it died. End of story.

Sometimes I don't mind that simple response, but also, I approach veganism from a rational and logical frame of thinking. So there needs to be more nuanced discussion on edge cases like this.

Eating roadkill is truthfully very different from eating a farmed animal -- and when it comes down to it, it may actually be an ethical action. Let's walk through the difference.

For traditionally farmed animal to get onto your plate, you (in most cases) paid someone for the meat. That exchange of money incentivizes the farmer (and the animal agriculture industry in general) to continue raising and slaughtering future animals. It's a matter of supply and demand. If people demand a product (which you do by purchasing it), the people who want your money will continue to provide it. And in a more direct sense, when you take from the supply of meat, more meat must be produced to keep up the supply for other people[6]. In the world of animal agriculture, this unfortunately means the continuation of the exploitation of animals and the cause of unnecessary suffering and early death for those animals.

But the roadkill, on the other hand, is completely isolated from the economics of the animal agriculture industry. If you choose to consume the meat of that deer, any moral dilemmas are (mostly) contained within the bubble of you and the deer. You aren't sending a signal out to anyone that you want them to keep killing more animals.

In this way, it would indeed be better if you only ever ate road-killed meat. You wouldn't be paying for any kind of animal exploitation. (And presumably you wouldn't be influencing drivers to purposefully hit more deer so you could eat them. If so, then that would be an exploitation situation. You would be causing pain to the animal and taking its life, for your own benefit, when you do not need to.)

And yet, even if road-kill is ethical compared to farmed animal, I personally would still never eat meat in this situation. Why?

I honestly have not thought super deeply about this topic before. But my instinct is that it still just... feels wrong. After being vegan for five years, I feel no desire to consume the flesh of an animal. I seem to have developed this gut-feeling aversion to viewing the carcass of a once-living creature as being food at all. I would feel the same way if the hypothetical were about an accidentally-killed cow or pig or etc. rather than a deer.

Plus, a big reason for staying vegan for me is the health benefits of eating a whole-food plant-based diet. So all ethical points aside, I still wouldn't want to incorporate this hypothetical roadkill situation into my diet. But again, I feel no desire.

But I guess I have to acknowledge that if someone approached me and asked if it's okay for them to eat roadkill, the answer would have to be yes. They genuinely are not hurting anyone by doing it. (My own caveat here would be that by consuming an animal product, they are still promoting the idea of eating animal products to other people in society, which can contribute to the continuation of traditional animal exploitation.)

Back to the spaghetti people

As I was saying, at the start of the Rick and Morty episode, the aliens who commit suicide chose to die.

So it it ethical to eat them?

Well, similar to the roadkill situation, you are doing no harm by eating them. They are already dead.

And yet, something still feels wrong. The person did not give consent to be eaten upon their death. This would be similar, in our world, to someone's body being used for research after they died (though, this seems like its own nuanced subject that I won't dive deeper into here).

We do see engagement with this thought in the episode. Morty is invited back to the planet and is shown a video of another citizen, who was terminally ill, stating that they desire to be eaten after they perform self-euthanasia. This is explicit consent, so I'd say this is the most ethical way to eat a spaghetti-person[7].

But then, as often happens in this show, things take a turn for the worse.

The government of the planet realizes that they can profit off of the spaghetti-turning biology. Since spaghetti is only manifested after suicide, they start to make the conditions of the planet incredibly depressing. They blot out the sun so it is gray and faded. They televise only bad reality tv. Their billboards promote self-sacrifice (to be someone's food) as something valiant.

The planet has turned into a factory farm, and in the government's (dollar-sign) eyes, the planet is thriving.

Pop quiz. Is this exploitation?

Answer: Yes.

Dictionary.com says: "Exploitation is the act of selfishly taking advantage of someone or a group of people in order to profit from them or otherwise benefit oneself."

The government is exploiting the people for its own profit.

Is it morally acceptable to consume the spaghetti from the exploited people? No! Someone purchasing the spaghetti is adding to the demand and thus will lead to the government continuing to devalue the life of the citizens and essentially coerce them into suicide. This is the strongest parallel to real-world animal agriculture that I'm sensing in this episode (even if there is a nuanced difference with this suicide caveat).

And finally, the end of the episode (and Rick's solution to the problem) brings the topic to a close, with yet another analogue to vegan ideas.

Turning away from the spaghetti industry

Rick decides he needs to put an end to the spaghetti-from-people industry. He locates a spaghetti-man who is close to his natural death, and offers him the chance to stop the spaghetti industry through his euthanasia. Rick plugs the man up to a fancy machine which, right before the man's self-inflicted death, projects the man's lifetime of memories to the people of the planet (and presumably all would-be spaghetti-consumers, who were lining up to buy more people-spaghetti). The projection depicts the most significant and emotional moments of the man's life, including falling in love, getting married, and the passing of his wife.

The man dies. Rick then slices open the man's belly and offers Morty the "delicious" spaghetti. Morty glances at it ... and then immediately vomits. Many who had been watching the video also vomits.

The spaghetti has not changed, but Morty, and all of the prior spaghetti-consumers, have. Suddenly, the idea of eating the spaghetti (or having eaten it previously) has become so revolting that it's vomit-inducing. It's clear that they will never consume the spaghetti again.

What happened?

With the pure, unfiltered video of the dying man's life-moments, the would-be spaghetti-consumers were granted a new perspective. It forced them to internalize the truth that the spaghetti-people are not just soon-to-be-spaghetti vessels to be eaten; they were real people who had a life experience just like the consumers.

The thing is, there was never secrecy around the way the spaghetti was generated. The consumers knew that the people had to die of suicide in order for them to get their spaghetti. But they didn't care, and consumed from the industry anyway. It took a change of perspective for them to re-think (maybe subconsciously) the feeling of desire for the "food".

Morty: You couldn’t change everyone’s taste, but you could make it… distasteful. It wasn’t the death, was it?

Rick: It was the complexity of life.

Morty hits an important point -- even though the people may still think the spaghetti tastes good[8], something mental has shifted that makes them view it no longer as desirable food. (Similar to my point in the interlude about the gut-instinct undesirability of road-killed deer meat even if it technically it could be considered ethical.)

Re-thinking food in our own world

It's not hard to draw the parallel from the episode to the real world. Becoming vegan is to re-think where our food came from. Most of us are born into a society where consuming animal products is a normal thing which almost everyone around us does, and there is no reason to question it. That is, until something makes us re-think it. For me, it was a video of Ed Winters talking about the philosophy of veganism. For others, they may chance upon a Cube of Truth demonstration and see the gory footage of the animal industry.

Whatever plants the seed in a person's mind, they stop seeing their (animal-based) food as just food. It came from an animal who was previously alive, and who had an experience of life. It may be a very different experience of life than humans have, but we come to understand that animals can have emotions, can be playful, can feel bonds with fellow animals (including humans!), and, above all, we see that they can experience pain and suffering.

None of that should sound surprising. We all know these things. And yet, just like the spaghetti-eaters, we don't think about it, or don't care, or don't see it as something to question. But when we connect the dots between the food on our plate and the animal that it used to be[9], this new perspective can make the food suddenly distasteful. And this can be enough for a person to start changing their choices around food.

Rick as activist

In a strange way[10], Rick was being an activist. He forced people to confront where their food came from, and made a real difference. This isn't too different from what vegan activists aim to do when they have open conversation with non-vegans to try to get them to see a new perspective on the systems of exploitation in our society.

Final thoughts

I enjoyed thinking more deeply about this episode and exploring the parallels which instinctively were obvious to me (but which were not fully formed in my mind until I actually went through the process of writing this). Great example of deeper meaning that can be extracted in media, and the value of contemplating it. This was fun! I'm glad I have this digital garden as a place to motivate me to do things like this. One of the earliest things I read about digital gardens / personal sites / blogs in general was encouraging people to do a talk-back to media you consume. To directly respond to what you've consumed is probably the most direct way to follow the Create More Than You Consume advice.

  1. no, nobody has asked these questions ↩︎

  2. An example of this that baffles me is the movie Chicken Run. The movie is about chickens on a farm that are trying to escape being turned into meat pies. The movie has real emotion and it's driven by making the viewer empathetic toward the chickens' survival. And, with a very small sample size on my end, for some people it does not even cross their mind that this may be related to the topic of veganism. ↩︎

  3. technically.... we need to know if these aliens can have viable offspring with humans to really classify them as a different species. But, please. They aren't human. (Maybe there is another perspective to this, though.) ↩︎

  4. taken conveniently from https://rickandmorty.fandom.com/wiki/That's_Amorte/Transcript ↩︎

  5. "unnecessary" because humans can survive+thrive on a fully plant-based diet ↩︎

  6. Obviously your one hamburger does not literally correspond to another fraction of a cow needing to be killed, but it adds up in the grander scheme. How many less cows would need to die during your lifespan if you personally never ate another hamburger? ↩︎

  7. ... in case you were considering doing so. ↩︎

  8. semi-related: Why do I stay vegan enough though I miss certain foods? ↩︎

  9. or, for animal-derived products like milk and eggs, think about the animal that had to suffer to produce it and eventually was still killed earlier than its normal lifespan due to being part of the industry ↩︎

  10. (...if we ignore that he himself continued to eat the spaghetti) ↩︎

entry.title: Dream Goal Build Civilization
entry.content:
It's more of a dream project than a goal -- this would be a long-spanning thing over many dreams. Equally as importing as experiencing it is writing+documenting it. This goal has served as a strong point of motivation that gets me looking forward to mastering my dreams, because I think it would be so cool to do this.

The task

The way I've envisioned it in my head: in a dream, I establish a persistent realm[1]. In that realm, I travel back in time to a world where there has been very little technological advancements, no cities, no civilizations. Perhaps just hunter-gatherer tribes of humans. Then the task is to meet these people, and help give them a head start on building up an advanced society.[2]

I think it would be really fun to build this up over time. I could go to the dream civilization, give them some help or teach them something, then come back in a later dream (or jump forward in time) and see how this tip I've given has changed their society. The cool thing is that I couldn't really predict how anything will go -- it's up to my mind (subconsciously) to decide the result of things. And I get to figure out how to respond to those results. In theory, it's an infinitely generated open-world video game in my mind.

Status on this task

Frankly, as of 2026 (13 years after I first discovered the concept of LDing), I feel very far from achieving anything close to this. But also, I don't think it is necessarily such an unrealistic task that it's not something I'll be able to do once I have consistent and high quality lucid dream experiences.

Mainly, I feel that I have a lot of foundational work to do in my dreams before I get to this point. There are the fundamentals of dream stability and confidence that I've struggled with for years. Then there is dream control and dream skills which I'd need, e.g. to transport myself to a persistent realm and be able to navigate it confidently, to travel forward (or backwards) in time, and so on.

Context / inspiration

My past self from November 2018 wrote this in Google Keep:

HUGE LD goal
Build civilization, following How to Invent Everything

How to Invent Everything is a book by Ryan North that talks at a high level about, well, pretty much how to re-build civilization from scratch.

That book's subtitle is "A survival guide for the stranded time traveler". I remember reading the intro to the book, which in a humorous way talks about this (obviously fictional) scenario where you are a time traveler and go back in time and get stranded and want to rebuild civilization.

I don't quite remember if my dream goal actually came as a result of reading some snippets of this book. But it's possible that it did. Even before the book, though, I generally had in mind that I was very excited to generally learn about how things work, and how things got to how they are. That general interest is what led to this book catching my eye. Then I think this book inspired the dream goal.

So yeah -- I've had this dream goal floating around in my mind for a while, and I've never acted on it. But it's come to be one of the strongest motivators for lucid dreaming for me. I think it would be so cool for me to pursue this as sort of a dream project.

Persistent Realms

A key aspect of this dream goal is the idea of persistent realms. Building a civilization takes time! And probably many, many dream sessions. And that's the fun part. It's a long-term project. The world where I'm building civilization needs to be persistent across many dream sessions so that it can build up over time. Otherwise, it would be like building a Minecraft world, but every time you close the game, the entire world is wiped. You need to save the state of the world between sessions. That's the idea behind persistent realms.

Related stuff

  • Youtube video: "How To Make WIFI Starting With Only A Rock" (channel: Rune). I came across this video, and it's what motivated me to add this page to my digital garden! It's a fun video and obviously reminded me of this dream goal.

  1. (see section below for more on "persistent realms") ↩︎

  2. As I write this... I am realizing how I sound like a colonizer. But it's not about forcing my own ways/beliefs on these (dream character!) people. It's about improving the quality of life for them. ↩︎
